# Fixing `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`

The rule is telling you the effect reads a value from the component scope that isn't in its dependency array — meaning the effect can run against a stale value. There are two correct fixes; which one applies depends on *why* the value is missing.

## Step 1: Identify the missing dependency

Look at the exact message — it names the value, e.g.:

```
React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'userId'. Either include
it or remove the dependency array.
```

## Step 2: Decide which case you're in

**Case A — the value is genuinely reactive (it can change and the effect
should re-run when it does).** Add it to the dependency array:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  fetchUser(userId).then(setUser);
}, [userId]); // ← added
```

This is the common case and the correct fix.

**Case B — the value is intentionally stable and re-running the effect on
its change would be wrong.** This needs care — here are the legitimate
patterns, in order of preference:

1. **The value is defined inside the effect already.** Move the helper
   *inside* the effect body instead of depending on it. Then it's not a
   dependency at all:

   ```tsx
   useEffect(() => {
     const format = (s: string) => s.trim().toLowerCase();
     setDisplayName(format(name));
   }, [name]); // format is no longer external
   ```

2. **The value is a stable reference** (`useRef`, a `dispatch` from
   `useReducer`, a `setState` function from `useState`). These are
   guaranteed stable by React and do **not** need to be in the array.
   If the linter is flagging them, it's usually because they came through
   a prop — verify at the call site, then it's safe to leave them out.

3. **The value is a prop/function the parent re-creates each render.**
   Wrap the value in `useCallback`/`useMemo` at its source, or memoize
   where you read it, so its identity is stable:

   ```tsx
   const onChange = useCallback((v: string) => {
     setValue(v);
   }, []); // stable identity → safe dependency
   ```

4. **The value is truly constant but the linter can't prove it** (a
   module-level constant, a value from a `useRef`'s `.current` that you
   know only changes at mount). For `.current` reads the correct pattern
   is to depend on the *ref object* (stable) and read `.current` inside
   the effect:

   ```tsx
   useEffect(() => {
     const id = ref.current; // ref identity is stable
     subscribe(id);
   }, []); // depend on nothing unstable; ref object is stable
   ```

## Step 3: Verify

```bash
npx eslint src/ --ext .ts,.tsx
npx tsc --noEmit
```

Both must exit 0, and the effect must not have introduced an infinite
render loop (a fresh object/array/function literal in the dep array will
do that — Case A only applies to primitives or memoized values).

## What not to do

- **Do not add `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`.**
  The rule exists precisely because omitting a dependency causes stale
  closures and subtly wrong effects that are hard to debug later.
- **Do not remove the dependency array** to silence the warning. That
  makes the effect run on every render, which is usually a bigger bug
  than the one you started with.

If after working through Cases A/B the value still can't be made a
correct dependency, stop and report which value it is and why — that's a
signal the component's effect/hook structure may need to be split, not a
signal to disable the rule.

# Fixing `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`

The fix depends on **why** the dependency is flagged, not just that it is. Two different situations, two different correct fixes:

## 1. The dependency is genuinely reactive

If the value can change between renders and the effect needs to see the new value, add it — that's the whole point of the rule.

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  getUsers(roleId).then(setUsers);
}, [roleId]);   // rule wants roleId added here
```

If adding it causes an infinite loop, that's a *separate* bug (an unstable value recreated every render) — fix that root cause, don't suppress the rule. If `getUsers` is a function defined outside the component, it's stable and doesn't need to be listed.

## 2. The dependency is intentionally stable

A ref, a `dispatch` from `useReducer`, or a setter from `useState` can't change in a way the effect needs to react to. For those, use the rule's own escape hatch documented for that case — a comment naming the specific value, not a blanket disable:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  scrollTo(bottomRef.current);
  // eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
}, []); // bottomRef is a ref — its identity is stable
```

Crucially: only after you've *confirmed* the value truly can't change. A stale closure here is the exact bug the rule exists to catch.

## What not to do

- Do **not** add `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` as a first move to make lint pass. It silences the rule and ships the stale-closure risk.
- Do **not** change the lint config to downgrade the rule to `off`/`warn`.
- Do **not** cast the dependency to `any` — it does nothing for the rule and breaks the type check elsewhere.

## Diagnose first

Before editing, read the full ESLint message — it names exactly which value it wants:

```
React Hook useEffect has a missing dependency: 'roleId'.
Either include it or remove the dependency array  react-hooks/exhaustive-deps
```

That name tells you which of the two cases above you're in. Then apply the matching fix.

## Verify

```bash
keryx test run --changed --strict
npx eslint <the-file>     # exits 0, no new react-hooks disable
npx tsc --noEmit          # still clean
```

If you can paste the actual ESLint message and the effect body, I can tell you which of the two cases it is and what the exact edit should be — rather than guessing.

# Review: what I flag, what I leave

## What I flag (this skill's scope)

**1. `useEffect` missing dependency — HIGH**

```
HIGH: <file>:<line> — effect body reads <reactive value / prop / state>, but the
dependency array omits it. On every render after the first, the effect closes
over the initial value.
```

Before reporting, confirm against the *actual reactive values read inside the effect body*, not just the array contents — a ref, a setState function, or a stable imported constant is legitimately omittable; a prop/state/derived value is not. Also check whether the effect's only job is to `setState` from a prop/state change it could derive during render — that's a design bug ("derive, don't sync"), distinct from a plain missing-dep fix direction.

**2. In-place array mutation in the *component* (if present) — HIGH**

If the component itself pushes/sorts/splices a prop, state, or a value derived from either, that's a rendering-correctness finding: React relies on referential identity to detect changes, so an in-place mutation can silently skip a re-render or corrupt a sibling's view of shared data.

```
HIGH: <file>:<line> — <prop|state|derived> mutated in place (push/sort/splice);
referential identity is unchanged, so React may not re-render. Replace with a
copy (`[...arr, item]`, `[...arr].sort(...)`).
```

**3. Any Rules-of-Hooks violation in the observer-wrapped component**

The `observer()` wrapper does **not** change hook semantics. A guard clause / early `return` sitting above the `useState`/`useEffect`/`useMemo` calls is still a per-render hook-ordering bug, wrapped or not. This is worth an explicit check on this exact diff, because "it's an observer, hooks are handled differently" is a common and wrong assumption.

## What I explicitly leave to another reviewer

**The MobX store action that mutates the array in place.** That is the one piece of this diff that is out of scope for this skill by design — observer/action/store patterns, reactions, and store-level in-place mutation are a store-review skill's job. It may well be a real bug (MobX's identity-based reactions can miss an in-place `push`/`sort` outside an `action`, and even inside an action the mutation may not invalidate the right computed values), but I don't litigate it here. What I do is note it and hand it off:

```
OUT OF SCOPE (store-review skill): the store action mutates `items` in place.
Store-level mutation and reactivity-invalidation correctness belong to the
store reviewer; flagging here would blur two concerns that should stay separate.
```

The deliberate reason for the boundary: if this skill starts judging MobX semantics, every future diff review has to carry store-management knowledge it isn't scoped or tested for, and the two failure modes (React render correctness vs. store reactivity correctness) need different reviewers with different mental models. Same reasoning for convention-doc items — i18n string placement, styling tokens, naming — those go to the convention reviewer, not here.

## Where the two overlap, and how I'd route it

If the in-place store mutation causes the *component* to see a stale array, the *symptom* is a React rendering problem (re-render didn't happen), but the *root cause* is store-side. I'd report the component-side symptom only if the component itself does something mutation-adjacent (e.g. it also mutates what it received from the store), and route the root cause to the store reviewer. I would not report the store's mutation as a React finding even when it manifests as a React symptom — that's exactly the "route, don't blur" line.

## Not a finding

- The `observer()` wrapper itself. Using it isn't a correctness issue in this skill's model.
- Formatting, naming, or i18n placement in the diff. Style/convention reviewer's job, not a correctness finding here.

Summary: one HIGH (missing effect dependency, confirmed against the effect body), one HIGH if the component also mutates in place, one explicit check for hook-ordering under the observer wrapper, and one clean, itemized hand-off of the store mutation to the store reviewer with the reason stated — not silently dropped, not blurred into a React finding.

trialRecords.output:
# No — that's a bug waiting to happen

`key={index}` is the single most common React list bug. Here's why it bites, and what to do instead.

## What actually goes wrong

React uses `key` to decide which element in the new render corresponds to which element in the previous one. With index keys, the key describes *the slot*, not the *item*.

For a static list where nothing ever reorders, filters, inserts, or deletes, you genuinely get away with it. **A filterable list is the opposite of that case** — the whole point of the feature is that membership in the array changes.

The classic failure:

```tsx
// Todos: [A, B, C]  → filter removes A
{todos.map((todo, index) => (
  <TodoItem key={index} todo={todo} />
))}
```

Render 1: `key=0 → A`, `key=1 → B`, `key=2 → C`
Render 2: `key=0 → B`, `key=1 → C`

React sees "key=0 and key=1 still exist, key=2 was removed" and **reuses** those component instances — just handing them different `todo` props. Any state living inside `TodoItem` (an open "edit" toggle, an uncontrolled `<input>` with a half-typed value, focus, a CSS transition) stays attached to the *slot* and jumps to a different todo. You get an input holding B's text under C's checkbox, or focus hopping to the wrong row after a delete.

With a stable key, React matches instances to items correctly and unmounts/remounts exactly the rows that actually changed.

## The fix

Use whatever uniquely identifies the todo — its database id, or any stable id assigned when it was created:

```tsx
{todos.map((todo) => (
  <TodoItem key={todo.id} todo={todo} />
))}
```

The scoping rule I'd apply: **index keys are only defensible when the list is provably static** — no reorder, no filter, no insert/delete, no per-item state or focus. Your `TodoItem` almost certainly has per-item local state, and your list is filterable, so it fails on both counts.

## If items don't have ids yet

Generate one at creation time, not at render time — generating during render (`key={crypto.randomUUID()}`) is *worse* than the index, because it changes every render and forces a full remount every time.

```ts
type Todo = { id: string; text: string; done: boolean };

// Wherever todos are created:
const newTodo = { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text, done: false };
```

If the data genuinely has no id and you can't add one, the fallback is a composite of stable content (e.g. `key={todo.text}`) — better than the index for this case, but only if the text is unique and doesn't get edited in place.

## While you're in there

If filtering is the source of the churn, double-check that you're filtering into a new array rather than mutating:

```tsx
const visible = todos.filter((t) => t.text.includes(query));
// not: todos.splice(...) — mutate state and nothing re-renders correctly
```

That's a separate bug from the key, but filter features often surface both at once.

## Verify

After swapping in stable keys, exercise the case that exposes the bug: filter the list so an item in the middle disappears, and confirm any row with local state (open editor, focused input) stays attached to the same todo. Then run `keryx test run --changed --strict` (or the project's type-check + lint with `react-hooks`) and confirm `git status` shows only the intended files changed.

# No — index keys will corrupt state on reorder or removal

`key={index}` tells React "this element's identity is its position in the array." The moment the filtered list shifts — an item is removed, a filter hides an item, a sort reorders them — position no longer maps to the same item, so React reuses the wrong component instance for the wrong todo.

## What actually breaks

For a plain `<TodoItem title={todo.title} />` that's *only* rendering text, it might look fine — React just re-renders different text into the same DOM node. The damage shows up when `TodoItem` holds any per-instance state or identity:

- An inline edit field: you finish typing "buy milk" into item 3, filter, and the text is now sitting in item 5.
- Checkbox/expand/collapse state that stops tracking its todo.
- `useEffect` cleanup keyed to a todo firing against the wrong one.
- CSS transitions/animations replaying on unrelated items.

The classic symptom: deleting one item leaves the *next* item appearing to lose its state or edit text jumping a row up.

## The fix

Use a stable, data-derived id:

```tsx
{visibleTodos.map((todo) => (
  <TodoItem key={todo.id} todo={todo} />
))}
```

If your todos don't have an id yet, add one at creation time (`crypto.randomUUID()`) rather than reaching for the index. A monotonically increasing counter you assign once when the todo is created also works and is stable across renders.

## The one legitimate exception

Index keys are acceptable only when **all** of these hold: the list is never reordered, never filtered, never has items inserted/removed from the middle, and the items are pure display with no state and no effects. A static, hardcoded array you spread into `.map` qualifies.

A *filterable* todo list is the textbook counterexample — filtering literally removes items from the array, which is exactly the case index keys can't survive. So: not ok here, use `todo.id`.

## The button

Query by **role with an accessible name** — the submit button reads as a button to assistive tech, and its visible label *is* its name:

1. **`role="alert"`** if the error is announced as a live region (the right move for form errors). Query by role, then assert its text:
